stories.title: Observer Media Relocates Offices to 1330 Avenue of the Americas
stories.excerpt: Commercial Observer writes tenaciously about Midtown’s office market. Now, it’s joining the action. Observer Media, the digital media company home to Commercial Observer and the Observer, is relocating its offices to 1330 Avenue of the Americas, a 40-story office building owned by a joint venture involving Creed Equities, Hakimian Capital, CH Capital Group and Nassimi Realty. Observer will move in December from its current offices at 1 Whitehall Street in the Financial District. MetroLoft Management has plans to convert the office property into residential rental apartments. The media company’s new Midtown office will span 16,400 square feet across the entire third floor of 1330 Avenue of the Americas, situated between West 53rd and West 54th streets, across the street from Midtown’s Hilton hotel. Observer is subleasing the space through February 2031 from home design company MillerKnoll, which is consolidating its space to its other New York City location at 251 Park Avenue South. Asking rent for the sublease was in the $60s per square foot, while rents in the rest of the building range between $80 to $120 per square foot, according to CBRE’s Arkady Smolyansky, who represented Observer Media in the deal alongside Jacob Rosenthal. Cushman & Wakefield’s Justin Royce, Harrison Dubin and Amy Sola brokered the sublease deal for MillerKnoll. A spokesperson for C&W did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Isabelle Durso can be reached at idurso@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Observer Media subleasing 16,400 SF at 1330 Avenue of the Americas, Midtown Manhattan through Feb 2031
MetroLoft Management converting office property to residential apartments; office-to-residential pipeline continues
Sublease asking rent ~$60/SF; indicates office space still commanding rents despite conversion plans
stories.summary: Observer Media is relocating from the Financial District to a 16,400-SF sublease on the third floor of 1330 Avenue of the Americas in Midtown, occupying space through February 2031. The property owner plans to convert the office building to residential rental apartments. The sublease—from MillerKnoll, which is consolidating operations—reflects continued office market activity amid broader office-to-residential conversion trends in Manhattan.
stories.impact: Office-to-residential conversions accelerate supply of rental apartments in Midtown Manhattan and Midtown South, improving new supply availability but signaling weak office demand fundamentals. Expect rental rates to reflect conversion economics—typically Class B/C product priced below new construction. This conversion asset class competes directly with new multifamily development on yield and rent assumptions in tight NYC submarkets.

stories.title: Location, Timing, Connection Drove World Cup Gains in Host Cities
stories.excerpt: For the 11 host markets across the U.S., the 2026 FIFA World Cup brought millions of fans – and with them, high expectations of a summer boom for local retailers, restaurants, and property owners. While the tournament delivered a substantial economic boost, foot traffic data reveals a more nuanced picture, Placer.ai says in a new white paper. “Host markets saw only a marginal metro-wide retail lift and a modest dining lift over the course of the tournament,” according to the white paper, 7 World Cup Lessons for Retail, Dining & Real Estate, produced by Placer.ai and Colliers. “Instead, the real gains flowed to the businesses and properties most closely tied to the fan journey – the right location, the right timing, and a clear connection to the event.” Specifically, event demand was hyperlocal, with retail and dining gains concentrated near stadiums and dropping off sharply for locations farther away from the World Cup sites. And though central stadiums channeled traffic into existing commercial districts, some markets showed that well-placed fan destinations can extend an event’s economic footprint beyond the venue. The post Location, Timing, Connection Drove World Cup Gains in Host Cities appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: 2026 FIFA World Cup in 11 U.S. host markets showed hyperlocal retail and dining gains near stadiums
Economic benefits concentrated within walking distance of venues; foot traffic dropped sharply beyond stadium zones
Mixed-use and proximity strategy: well-placed fan destinations extended event's economic footprint beyond venue perimeter
stories.summary: Placer.ai analysis of 2026 FIFA World Cup's impact on 11 U.S. host markets reveals retail and dining gains were highly concentrated near stadiums, with foot traffic and economic benefit declining sharply away from venues. Marginal metro-wide retail lift and modest dining lift overall; the real gains flowed to properties with direct connection to fan journey. Strategic location and mixed-use positioning extended economic benefits beyond the stadium footprint.
stories.impact: For multifamily developers in World Cup host markets (likely includes Dallas, LA, Miami, Atlanta, others), dense mixed-use neighborhoods adjacent to venue zones will outperform outlying areas. Demonstrates that event-driven demand is temporary and hyperlocal—anchor multifamily near complementary retail/dining/hospitality nodes to capture spillover, not mid-market residential far from action. Model applies to any major event infrastructure investment.

stories.title: Urban Outfitters–Leased Retail Condo in Wicker Park Changes Hands
stories.excerpt: Greenstone Partners has completed the sale of 1521 N. Milwaukee Ave., a 10,600-square-foot, two-level retail condominium in Chicago’s Wicker Park neighborhood that is 100% leased to Urban Outfitters. The property sold for $4.125 million. Managing Partner Danny Spitz and Partner Brewster Hague represented the seller, Newcastle Investors, a longtime owner of retail properties in the neighborhood. Spitz also brokered Newcastle’s acquisition of the property in 2013. Urban Outfitters has occupied the property since 2005, making it one of the first national retailers to plant a flag in Wicker Park. The ground and second-floor space includes an additional 2,676-square-foot lower level and about 50 feet of frontage on Milwaukee Avenue. Nearby retailers include Barnes & Noble, Adidas Originals, Levi’s, Abercrombie & Fitch, Wells Fargo, Carhartt, CAVA, sweetgreen and Supreme. The post Urban Outfitters–Leased Retail Condo in Wicker Park Changes Hands appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Greenstone Partners sold 10,600-SF, two-level Urban Outfitters retail condo in Chicago's Wicker Park for $4.125M
100% leased; Urban Outfitters anchor tenant since 2005; nearby retail includes Barnes & Noble, Adidas, CAVA, Sweetgreen
Strong retail fundamentals in neighborhood support mixed-use redevelopment signals and ground-floor activation near residential
stories.summary: Greenstone Partners completed the sale of 1521 N. Milwaukee Ave., a 10,600-SF retail condo in Wicker Park, Chicago, for $4.125 million. Urban Outfitters has anchored the fully occupied property since 2005. The neighborhood's retail corridor includes national brands and dining concepts, indicating sustained demand and foot traffic.
stories.impact: Wicker Park's retail resilience and anchor-tenant stability signal strong underlying residential demand in the neighborhood. For multifamily developers, this validates ground-floor retail activation strategy in mixed-use projects nearby; strong retail fundamentals support higher residential rents and walkability premiums. Retail-anchored neighborhood desirability should inform site selection and pro-forma assumptions for new residential development in Wicker Park and similar gentrifying Chicago neighborhoods.

stories.title: Sterling Bay Achieves Full Retail Occupancy at 123 N. Wacker
stories.excerpt: Sterling Bay announced that retail at 123 N. Wacker Drive in Chicago’s central business district has reached 100% occupancy. “Along with ownership, we’ve invested in creating a truly compelling environment that tenants and neighbors are clearly responding to, proving that strategically curating the right mix of office, retail and amenities will draw people to the building and drive long-term value,” said Austin Lusson, Director, Leasing at Sterling Bay.The property’s retail tenants include ESPRESSO AND MILK, opening its second location in the south retail space this fall, and Just Salad, which will occupy the northwest retail space. First Independence Bank is taking the northeast retail space in addition to office space upstairs in the office tower.Sterling Bay has served as leasing, property and asset management at 123 N. Wacker since 2024. Beyond retail, Sterling Bay has secured long-term leases for the property’s penthouse with Transwestern and the full 19th floor with CRC Group. The post Sterling Bay Achieves Full Retail Occupancy at 123 N. Wacker appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Sterling Bay achieved 100% retail occupancy at 123 N. Wacker Drive in Chicago's CBD
Tenants include ESPRESSO AND MILK (second location), Just Salad, First Independence Bank; mixed office/retail/amenity strategy
Full retail occupancy signals office building stabilization and mixed-use repositioning success in CBD
stories.summary: Sterling Bay announced 100% retail occupancy at 123 N. Wacker Drive in Chicago's central business district. The property features a curated retail and food-service mix including ESPRESSO AND MILK, Just Salad, and First Independence Bank, alongside office and amenity space. Sterling Bay credits strategic curation of office, retail, and amenities with driving tenant and neighbor engagement and long-term value.
stories.impact: Successful retail stabilization in CBD office building demonstrates that mixed-use programming—dining, banking, casual QSR—drives foot traffic and attracts office tenants, strengthening office demand. For multifamily developers considering CBD residential product, ground-floor retail and amenity activation is critical to competitiveness. Retail-forward office/residential mixed-use projects in Chicago CBD and similar urban cores should model amenity budgets and retail lease economics as essential to residential lease-up and rate sustainability.

stories.title: The South Florida Real Estate Market Leans Evermore on the Wealthy

Darrow, chairman and CEO of DarrowEverett. “There’s a new billionaire minted in San Francisco every week, and they want to be in Miami,” added Genghis Hadi, co-founder and managing principal of Nahla Capital, which is redeveloping Miami Beach’s oceanfront Raleigh hotel, its first project in South Florida. bullets: South Florida remains strong; wealthy Northerners continue relocation; multiple institutional term sheets for financing suggest capital availability
Dezer Development building Bentley condo tower in Sunny Isles Beach; Nahla Capital redeveloping Raleigh hotel oceanfront; Swire Properties broke ground on condo project
Pricing power at high-end: ultra-luxury condo market driven by billionaire in-migration from San Francisco; rising rates have not dampened wealth inflow
stories.summary: South Florida's real estate market remains resilient as wealthy Northerners—particularly from San Francisco—continue relocating south, driving ultra-luxury condo demand and multiple financing term sheets. Developers including Dezer Development (Bentley, Sunny Isles Beach), Nahla Capital (Raleigh Hotel oceanfront redevelopment), and Swire Properties are breaking ground on condo towers. Despite national headwinds from rising rates, high-end financing competition and capital availability remain strong.
stories.impact: South Florida's reliance on wealth migration creates bifurcated market: ultra-luxury condo product priced $2M+ attracts capital, while middle-market and workforce rental and ownership product faces tighter lending and fewer buyers. For multifamily developers, luxury rental assets in Miami, Miami Beach, Sunny Isles, and Brickell will command premium rents and cap-rate compression. Conversely, moderate-income multifamily in secondary South Florida submarkets faces headwinds. Market segmentation by income and buyer/renter profile is acute—underwrite accordingly by submarket and unit mix.

stories.title: Amazon Leases 91K-SF Warehouse in Everett
stories.excerpt: Amazon has leased a 90,970-square-foot warehouse in Everett for the company’s Leo satellite division. Two years after vacating a warehouse in Everett, Amazon⁠.com Inc. (Nasdaq: AMZN⁠) has returned to the building with a new lease, and the Seattle-based tech giant will occupy the industrial facility at 6611 Associated Blvd., reported the Puget Sound Business Journal. Amazon had occupied the industrial facility from at least 2018 until 2024, when it let the lease expire. The property hasn’t been physically occupied since at least 2022, and Colliers began marketing the property for lease in March of 2024. Located nearby is the 167,000-square-foot logistics hub for Amazon’s orbital satellite division, which was repurposed from a former delivery station. Amazon Leo, formerly known as Project Kuiper, is the company’s low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite broadband network. The subsidiary was established in 2019 to deploy a large satellite Internet constellation providing low-latency connectivity. The post Amazon Leases 91K-SF Warehouse in Everett appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Amazon leased 90,970-SF warehouse in Everett, WA (6611 Associated Blvd) for Leo satellite division
Amazon previously occupied facility 2018–2024; returning after two-year vacancy; nearby 167,000-SF logistics hub supports Leo orbital satellite operations
Leo (Project Kuiper) is low-Earth-orbit broadband subsidiary; expansion signals sustained tech investment and job creation in Seattle metro
stories.summary: Amazon leased a 90,970-square-foot warehouse in Everett, Washington for its Leo satellite division (Project Kuiper low-Earth-orbit broadband network). The company had previously occupied the facility from 2018 until 2024 and is now returning. Nearby operates Amazon's 167,000-SF logistics hub supporting Leo operations, indicating significant infrastructure investment and employment.
stories.impact: Amazon's re-commitment to Everett and Leo expansion signals sustained high-wage tech employment and capital deployment in Seattle metro's industrial/logistics corridor. Multifamily developers should monitor Leo's headcount trajectory and facility expansion; satellite and aerospace engineering jobs attract talent inflow. Everett submarket (north of Seattle) and adjacent Puget Sound communities should see residential demand uplift and rent growth as Amazon Leo scales. This is a leading indicator for both luxury and workforce housing demand in Everett/Lynnwood/Mill Creek submarkets over 2–4 years.

stories.title: Hanley Investment Group Arranges Sale of Milwaukee Shopping Center
stories.excerpt: Hanley Investment Group Real Estate Advisors arranged the sale of Cornerstone Shopping Center, a 13,308‑square‑foot retail center located in the North Shore trade area across from Bayshore, one of Wisconsin’s mixed‑use destinations. Hanley Investment Group’s Executive Vice President and Partner Jeff Lefko and Executive Vice President Bill Asher, in association with ParaSell, Inc., represented the seller, a private investor from North San Diego County, California. The buyer, SW Neighborhood Centers IV, an affiliate of Alabama-based commercial real estate firm Shannon Waltchack, represented itself. “We generated multiple competitive offers from private equity and institutional buyers within the first few weeks of marketing and secured an all‑cash institutional buyer that closed escrow in 45 days,” Lefko said. The property consists of two retail buildings totaling 13,308 square feet on 1.05 acres. It is located at 635‑695 West Silver Spring Drive and 5575‑5595 North Port Washington Road in Glendale, Wisconsin, and was 100% occupied at the time of the sale. The post Hanley Investment Group Arranges Sale of Milwaukee Shopping Center appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Hanley Investment Group arranged sale of Cornerstone Shopping Center (13,308 SF) in Glendale, Wisconsin near Bayshore mixed-use for undisclosed price
100% occupied at sale; buyer is SW Neighborhood Centers IV (Alabama-based Shannon Waltchack affiliate); all-cash institutional buyer closed in 45 days
Multiple competitive offers from private equity and institutional buyers; indicates strong neighborhood retail investment appetite
stories.summary: Hanley Investment Group brokered the sale of Cornerstone Shopping Center, a 13,308-SF retail center on 1.05 acres in Glendale, Wisconsin's North Shore trade area (near Bayshore mixed-use destination), to SW Neighborhood Centers IV. The property was 100% occupied and closed all-cash in 45 days, generating multiple competitive institutional and private equity offers.
stories.impact: North Shore Glendale retail market strength and investor appetite for stabilized, fully-leased neighborhood centers indicate strong underlying residential and commercial activity in Milwaukee suburbs. Multifamily developers should view Bayshore and North Shore as high-barrier, affluent submarkets with stable demographics and retail fundamentals supporting premium residential rents. Mixed-use development adjacent to retail centers like Cornerstone (or near Bayshore itself) benefits from established foot traffic and amenity ecosystem.

stories.title: A Third of Maturing Multifamily Debt Needs Cash Infusion to Refinance
stories.excerpt: After September’s rate hike, $6.8 billion of fresh equity stands between maturing multifamily loans and a refinance. Loans written at 2021 and 2022’s low coupons are the hardest hit. 20 Exchange Place, a 54-story, 767-unit apartment tower near Wall Street that was built in 1929, was 94 percent occupied in the second quarter, and its loan is current. But the $246 million Freddie Mac loan behind it carries a 4.01 percent coupon and matures in February 2027. The property’s 2025 net operating income of $15.5 million would support a new loan of about $183 million at today’s agency rates, leaving a gap of roughly $63 million. The borrower has been calling capital from investors as needed to cover operating shortfalls, according to servicer commentary. That arithmetic is now common. CRED iQ resized every multifamily loan in Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and commercial mortgage-backed securities deals maturing between October 2026 and December 2028, $136 billion in all, at current new-issue coupons plus September’s rate hike. Nearly one in four (23 percent) of those loans, and 31 percent of the balance, could not refinance without new equity. Borrowers would need to bring $6.8 billion to the table. The median shortfall is 15 percent of the loan, or about $25,000 per apartment. What the hike did The Secured Overnight Financing Rate jumped from 3.62 percent to 3.85 percent on Sept. 17. Passed through to permanent loan coupons, the hike pushed 178 more loans ($4 billion of balance) below a 1.25 times coverage test and added $846 million to the equity gap. Each further 25 basis points adds roughly $1 billion more. Two more hikes would leave 39 percent of maturing multifamily debt short of a refinance. The gap is concentrated in loans written at the bottom of the rate cycle. Loans originated in 2021 and 2022, with a median coupon of 3.35 percent, now face refinancing rates roughly 2 to 3 percentage points higher. bullets: 23% of $136B multifamily loans maturing Oct 2026–Dec 2028; 31% of balance cannot refinance without new equity injection
Borrowers need $6.8B fresh equity infusion post-September rate hike; 2021–2022 low-coupon loans hit hardest; refinance gap widening
Example: 20 Exchange Place (54-story, 767-unit NYC tower) has $63M refinance shortfall on $246M Freddie Mac loan maturing Feb 2027
stories.summary: CRED iQ analysis shows $6.8 billion in fresh equity required for maturing multifamily loans between October 2026 and December 2028. Of $136 billion in loans analyzed, 23 percent of loans (31 percent by balance) cannot refinance at current agency rates without borrower equity infusion. Properties financed in 2021–2022 at low coupons face the largest gaps; example: 20 Exchange Place (NYC, 767 units) has a $63 million refinance shortfall on its $246 million Freddie Mac loan maturing February 2027.
stories.impact: Refinance crunch is accelerating forced capital calls, asset sales, and potential distressed sales in 2026–2027, particularly for 2021–2022 vintage stabilized assets. Multifamily developers and acquirers should prepare for temporary pricing dislocation and forced liquidations, creating acquisition windows in Q1 2027 onward. For new development underwriting, assume tighter exit financing and lower leverage (65–70% LTV max vs. historical 75%+); refinance risk is now a material underwriting assumption. Expect cap-rate compression and yield expansion to slow; focus capital on sponsorship strength and operational upside to justify equity checks.

stories.title: Stimdel Properties Files Plans to Build 612 Apartments in Astoria
stories.excerpt: Stimdel Properties, an affiliate of Uruguay-based investment firm HC Corporation, has filed plans to bring 612 new apartments to 12-12 33rd Avenue in Astoria, Queens, according to a rezoning application filed with New York City’s Department of City Planning last week. The plans, filed by Stimdel, call for the construction of five mixed-use buildings, ranging from five to nine stories tall, with a total of 50,000 square feet of commercial and manufacturing space. A portion of the 612 units will be designated as affordable housing, according to the project description. The site, located between 12th and 13th streets along 33rd Avenue in Queens, is currently home to several one-story industrial and office buildings. The landmarked Barkin, Levin & Company Office Pavilion building adjacent to the development site would also be “retained” as part of the project, according to the filing. “The development site currently represents a nonconforming industrial use at the border of a residential area of Astoria,” Stimdel wrote in its filing. “The rezoning would allow redevelopment of this underutilized block for a mix of uses, including local retail, community facility space and a substantial number of affordable housing units, that will blend with surrounding residential and community facility uses to create a cohesive neighborhood.” The project description doesn’t include any information about proposed amenities for the residents. The application still needs to go through several steps ahead of approval, including a review by the City Planning Commission, a community board review and a review by the borough president. News of the filing comes after a pair of Queens-based developers — Dominick Acquista and Lorenzo Devardo — submitted plans last month to replace three industrial buildings at 31-29 Vernon Boulevard in Astoria with a new 20-story residential tower, as Commercial Observer reported at the time. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Stimdel Properties (HC Corporation, Uruguay) filed rezoning for 612 apartments in Astoria, Queens at 12-12 33rd Avenue
Five mixed-use buildings, 5–9 stories; 50,000 SF commercial/manufacturing; portion affordable; site currently industrial/office; landmark building retained
Astoria industrial-to-residential rezoning; ongoing Long Island City and Queens waterfront multifamily pipeline expansion
stories.summary: Stimdel Properties filed rezoning plans with NYC Department of City Planning to develop 612 apartments on 12-12 33rd Avenue in Astoria, Queens. The mixed-use project comprises five buildings ranging 5–9 stories with 50,000 SF of commercial and manufacturing space, a portion of units designated affordable. The site currently hosts industrial and office buildings; a landmarked office pavilion will be retained. Rezoning application filed to convert nonconforming industrial use to mixed-use residential.
stories.impact: Astoria rezoning signals ongoing industrial-to-residential conversion pipeline in Queens, adding density and rental supply to outer-borough market. For multifamily developers, Astoria remains high-barrier to entry (rezoning risk, affordable housing requirements, Landmarks Preservation Commission), but successful completion of 612-unit project validates longer-term demand and rent growth trajectory. Monitor rezoning approval timeline and affordable unit economics (inclusionary zoning caps rents on 15–25% of units, reducing blended yield). Astoria rental market should see 2–3 year lease-up window and rent pressure from new supply, then stabilization as demand absorbs units.

stories.title: Southern California Retail Markets Tighten as Tenant Demand Picks Up
stories.excerpt: Southern California’s retail real estate market continued to tighten in the third quarter of 2026, with positive net absorption and declining vacancy across much of the region, according to a new report released Monday from Colliers. Retail tenants absorbed about 757,600 square feet during the quarter across Los Angeles and Orange counties and the Inland Empire. Overall vacancy fell 12 basis points from the second quarter to 6.15 percent, while leasing activity totaled 2.5 million square feet. Average asking rents increased 1 cent from the previous quarter to $2.40 per square foot per month on a triple-net basis, and up 1.33 percent compared to last year. The Inland Empire led the region with 527,000 square feet of positive net absorption, bringing its year-to-date total to more than 1 million square feet. The market accounted for nearly 70 percent of the region’s third-quarter absorption, despite a 34 percent quarterly decline in leasing activity to 767,000 square feet. Vacancy in the Inland Empire fell 30 basis points to 6.9 percent, while asking rents bumped up to $1.88 per square foot. Community and neighborhood shopping centers drove demand, accounting for approximately 276,000 square feet of positive absorption and 476,000 square feet of leasing activity. Orange County recorded another strong quarter, with 180,000 square feet of positive absorption and 444,000 square feet of leasing activity. Vacancy declined 25 basis points to 3.55 percent, a five-year low, while average asking rents jumped 3 percent quarter-over-quarter to $2.65 per square foot. Power centers accounted for approximately 143,000 square feet of Orange County’s absorption, helping offset losses at lifestyle and theme-festival centers, which gave back 118,000 square feet. Meanwhile, Los Angeles County experienced more modest strength. Net absorption totaled just 50,000 square feet, down 77 percent from the previous quarter, although leasing activity remained relatively strong at 1.3
bullets: Southern California retail vacancy fell 12 basis points Q3 2026 to 6.15%; positive net absorption 757,600 SF across LA, Orange, Inland Empire
Inland Empire led region with 527,000 SF absorption (70% of regional total); vacancy fell 30 bps to 6.9%; asking rents $1.88/SF/month NNN
Regional asking rents rose 1.33% YoY to $2.40/SF/month; leasing activity 2.5M SF; tight supply and tenant demand picking up
stories.summary: Southern California retail markets tightened in Q3 2026, with positive net absorption of 757,600 SF across Los Angeles, Orange County, and Inland Empire, reducing regional vacancy by 12 basis points to 6.15 percent. The Inland Empire dominated absorption at 527,000 SF (70 percent of regional total), with vacancy declining 30 basis points to 6.9 percent. Average asking rents increased to $2.40/SF/month NNN (up 1.33 percent YoY), with Inland Empire rents at $1.88/SF/month.
stories.impact: Inland Empire retail tightening and positive absorption indicate logistics, distribution, and e-commerce demand remain robust, supporting continued industrial-to-residential mixed-use development in IE logistics corridors. For multifamily developers, retail-anchored mixed-use projects in Inland Empire benefit from improving retail fundamentals and foot-traffic recovery. Rising retail rents support higher-density, walkable residential units near retail nodes. Southern California multifamily pro-formas should model stronger ground-floor retail revenue and lower retail vacancy risk in Inland Empire vs. LA/OC. Ground-floor retail leasing assumptions can now support tighter underwriting and lower retail loss-factor budgets.
